subtopic: MoE / Compute, parameter, and imbalance properties
learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about MoE compute/parameter efficiency and imbalance from common misconceptions.
stem: A top-2 MoE model with E=8 experts replaces a dense FFN block. Select all correct statements. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: The total parameter count scales linearly with E (all E experts have their own weight matrices), and the compute per token scales with E as well because the router must compute a gating score against every expert.
Total parameter count scales linearly with E, but compute per token is roughly constant in E (top-k activated) plus a small O(E) gating cost. This is why MoE gives parameter-to-flop leverage.

In serving, load imbalance across experts is a real problem: with random routing the variance of tokens-per-expert scales as sqrt(B*N/E), which can cause hot experts to bottleneck the batched matmul. Capacity limits or expert-parallel load-balancing are needed.

MoE inference is always memory-bandwidth bound because every forward pass must load all E experts' weights from HBM; expert parallelism does not help because it only distributes the weight-loading cost, not the parameter footprint.

explanation: B is correct: activated compute is essentially k * (MLP FLOPs) per token, independent of E; only the router's O(D * E) gating adds an O(E) term. C is correct: routing skew is a well-documented serving problem addressed by capacity factors and load balancing. A is wrong: activated compute is O(k), not O(E). D is wrong: only the k selected experts' weights are actually needed on each device per token; expert parallelism distributes both weight storage and per-token weight-load bandwidth, provided routing keeps tokens local to the expert.

optionExplanations.B: Correct: parameter scales with E, activated compute stays at O(k).
optionExplanations.C: Correct: routing skew is a real serving problem.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: expert parallelism does help by distributing weights.

assumptions: Routing is roughly balanced under normal training; imbalance is a corner case, not the norm.
nonImplications: Does not imply MoE is always faster than dense at equal parameter count; imbalance and communication overheads can eat the win.
Does not imply MoE quality equals dense at equal parameter count; it usually differs.
